transcript:
HEADER: 2026-03-31 10:30 PT | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Sofia (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Anika (Redwood SE), Laura (PacketFlow Eng Mgr), Dev (PacketFlow BE), Chris (Head of Platform), Maya (SRE)

SUMMARY: quick sync on recent microburst experiments, first-token (TTFT) variance, streaming hedging and routing options; align on next test runs and docs to share.

TOPICS: results recap; TTFT vs streaming tradeoffs; sequence length/hedging rules; kernel selection and quantization; security/KMS question; plan for AB priority test.

---
00:00 Sofia: okay uh thanks everyone for joining the sync, I think we have about 50 minutes, we'll go through the microburst timelines and then Marcus will walk the kernel tradeoffs. um quick roll call?
00:10 Laura: yep Laura here, Dev here too, Chris and Maya are on.
00:14 Chris: yep hi all, thanks.
00:18 Sofia: sweet alright Marcus you wanna start with the experiment recap?
00:22 Marcus: yeah, cool. so we ran three configurations last week — baseline hosted variant, dedicated with small batch hedging, and a streaming-forward path with prefix cache. results are a bit noisy but high level: median TTFT for baseline was ~120ms, dedicated hedging dropped median to 85ms, streaming path had best median 70ms but tail spikes up to 800ms during microbursts.
00:45 Dev: sorry can you repeat the streaming tail number? 800ms? that seems high.
00:49 Marcus: yeah that's, that's what we saw on the capture, it's basically when we get a sudden 300 qps to a narrow set of keys and the streaming handshake serialized.
00:59 Laura: and how big were the sequences in those tests? our real traffic is mostly 16-48 tokens.
01:04 Marcus: mostly seqlen 32 on average, peak 64. we also ran a long form 128 test to see seqlen effects, where the streaming path held up pretty well but kernel switching introduced jitter.
01:18 Sofia: quick note — PacketFlow's traffic distribution matters here. you had a pretty heavy prefix reuse, right?
01:23 Dev: yes about 40% prefix reuse on helpdesk flows.
01:27 Marcus: that actually helps caching, so dedicated plus prefix cache reduced cost per token significantly, but in microburst the batcher fills unevenly and there's a stall.
01:36 Maya: is that the same place you saw the KV cache thrash? in our observability it looked like a bunch of small KV get/sets.
01:42 Marcus: we did see cache evictions, and some of the eviction behavior is because of the seqlen heterogeneity — long tails displace short contexts in the LRU, so next short requests miss and pay full cost.
01:55 Chris: right, that's our biggest concern — tail latency spikes cause frontend backpressure; we need consistency not just median improvements.
02:03 Sofia: absolutely. okay Marcus can you walk through the kernel options and recommended hedges?
02:08 Marcus: sure. so we have three candidate kernel strategies: 1) conservative single-kernel path tuned for low-variance, that's what we used in baseline; 2) hybrid kernel switching which optimizes for median but can switch at runtime by seqlen thresholds; 3) streaming-first fastpath which keeps the KV cache active and uses micro-batching but is more sensitive to bursts.
02:30 Dev: hybrid sounds promising but switching itself adds overhead, right? how big?
02:34 Marcus: we measured kernel switch overhead around 10-18ms per switch on the platform, but it depends on model layers and quant profile; switching too often adds noise so you want hysteresis rules.
02:46 Laura: hysteresis as in seqlen > X for Y ms before switching?
02:50 Marcus: exactly, plus allow only once-per-request so you don't oscillate. also you can pin short sequences to the conservative kernel and only route long ones to the high-throughput kernel.
03:01 Sofia: we recommended priority routing last week — heavy hitters get high-priority lanes. how did that perform?
03:06 Marcus: priority lanes reduced observed tail for critical routes by ~40% in the dedicated config, but it pushed latency into the lower-priority pool — so you still get overall degradation if load is saturated.
03:18 Maya: what's the failure mode if a priority lane saturates? do we have graceful fallback?
03:22 Marcus: yes, Redwood's routing can fallback to a compatible model variant or dedicated spill to another region; in the pilot we saw a brief failover where requests directed to a smaller quantized variant with slightly worse quality but preserved SLO. there was some transient packetflow where sessions retried and user saw small quality diff.
03:41 Dev: about quantization — you said smaller quant profiles for spillover. did you measure quality regressions?
03:45 Marcus: we ran evals against a 50-sample question set; top-line quality drop was 2-3% for 4-bit quant vs fp16, but for our helpdesk prompts the user-visible regression was minimal. still we want a protected prompt set to verify.
03:59 Chris: we'll want that prompt set, and the evals. please include known failure cases.
04:05 Sofia: noted — action item for Marcus to package the quant evals.
04:09 Marcus: yeah will do.

04:20 Laura: can I ask about streaming handshake — what's causing the 800ms spike? it feels like a lock somewhere.
04:25 Marcus: based on flame graphs it's the streaming connection multiplexing, specifically when many small requests map to the same connection and the per-connection write buffer blocks. we also saw increased syscall latency during those bursts, so the kernel scheduling in the host was part of it.
04:39 Maya: interesting — in our infra we do socket offloading, could interact. we can capture a packet trace.
04:44 Dev: we can run tcpdump for a couple hours during our afternoon ramp, we'll annotate times.
04:47 Marcus: perfect, that trace will tell us if it's backpressure on the app socket or Redis/KV thrash.

05:02 Sofia: quick pause — security questions we had last meeting: KMS integration and audit logs. Chris?
05:07 Chris: yeah SAML is in place, we need to see KMS proof-of-concept with our internal key wrapping. also retention windows for logs — we can't send raw PII to hosted service.
05:17 Sofia: Redwood can support customer-managed KMS and provide redacted audit trails; Marcus will share the SOC2 link and KMS snippet.
05:25 Marcus: i'll attach the redacted audit artifact, and the doc for envelope encryption. note that on private deploy we can avoid egress entirely.

05:36 Laura: back to perf — what are realistic p99 SLOs we can target after hedging?
05:41 Marcus: with priority routing + conservative kernel fallback we saw p99 around 350-420ms in our tests; with streaming-first path p99 can be volatile up to 800ms as mentioned. the dedicated-reserved pool with hedging got us to ~320ms p99.
05:56 Maya: is there recommended burst capacity buffer? like how much headroom to commit in Dedicated?
06:02 Marcus: we typically recommend 30-40% reserved buffer for microburst-prone workloads, or configure autoscale with rapid provisioning plus a small local cache to soak spikes.
06:12 Dev: autoscale rapid provision sounds good but slower than we'd like; do we have metrics on spin-up time?
06:16 Marcus: on Redwood Dedicated, spin-up of extra workers is ~45-90s depending on region, so autoscale helps but you'll need local hedging for <2s spikes.

06:30 Sofia: ok let's talk about the A/B test plan — objective is to validate priority lanes + kernel hysteresis reduces p99 without regressing correctness. timeframe?
06:37 Laura: we can do a gradual canary next week, want the telemetry to be instrumented.
06:41 Marcus: propose splitting 10% of traffic for 48 hours, measure TTFT, p50/p95/p99, and quality metrics from the eval set. Also collect microburst trace samples.
06:51 Chris: sounds good. we need a stop condition if quality drop >4% or p99 worsens for non-priority flows beyond 20%.
06:59 Marcus: noted, we'll bake that into the rollout.

07:10 Dev: one more question — sequence length heuristics: you mentioned pinning short sequences to conservative kernel; what's the threshold?
07:16 Marcus: initial suggestion is seqlen <= 32 -> conservative; seqlen >= 96 -> high-throughput; 33-95 -> evaluate recent rolling average and routing probability. this is tunable.
07:28 Laura: can we get the config as JSON or yaml we can drop into our router?
07:31 Marcus: yes I'll share the routing snippet and example config.

07:42 Sofia: timeline and owners recap — we want microburst traces by Apr 3, spreadsheet and cost model Apr 2, kernel doc Apr 4, A/B test in Apr 6-8 window.
07:53 Maya: confirm Apr 6 works for scheduling.
07:55 Chris: yep we can do Apr 6 start.

08:00 Sofia: any blockers from PacketFlow on security or legal?
08:04 Chris: legal wants redacted SOC2 and SLA terms — will need to review before dedicated commit.
08:10 Sofia: we'll surface SOC2 and standard SLA language, and Marcus will include KMS note.

08:18 Dev: I have a small ask — can we get a sample of the model variant used in the spillover so we can run local smoke tests?
08:24 Marcus: yes, we can publish a pinned model id and quant profile that you can pull from the catalog in staging.

08:32 Laura: ok last thing, can you summarize the expected cost impact of routing + hedging vs just increasing Dedicated capacity?
08:38 Sofia: short answer: hedging + caching typically reduces per-token cost 15-30% versus brute-forcing more GPUs, but you pay complexity and slightly higher ops. we'll put numbers in the sheet.
08:49 Marcus: and note there's a sweet spot — small amount of reserved capacity plus hedging gives most bang for buck.

09:00 Sofia: great, thanks everyone. quick recap of next steps (we'll email):
09:05 — Sofia: send latency/cost spreadsheet (due Apr 2)
09:07 — Marcus: kernel tradeoffs doc, quant evals, routing snippet (due Apr 4)
09:11 — Dev: 48h microburst capture (due Apr 3)
09:14 — Maya: redacted architecture and confirm KMS details (due Apr 5)

09:20 Chris: thanks all, we'll come back with schedule for the canary.
09:23 Sofia: awesome, end of sync. I'll follow-up with calendar invite for Apr 6 start window.
